1101.quote_or_event: “O my eyes, the Lord has infused His Light into you; do not look upon any other than the Lord.”
1101.explanation: In Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das speaks in turn to the body, the eyes and the ears, telling each sense that its true fulfilment lies in the Lord.
1101.tie_back: The Kural finds the joys of all five senses in one woman; Anand Sahib directs the senses one by one to the one Beloved, God.
1101.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 922, Raag Ramkali, Anand Sahib (pauri 36), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1101._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both gather the senses on a single beloved, but Anand Sahib turns the senses toward God and away from sensual pleasure, which is close to the opposite of the Kural's delight.

1102.quote_or_event: “The physician was called in; he touched my arm and felt my pulse. The foolish physician did not know that the pain was in the mind.”
1102.explanation: In a salok of Malar ki Vaar, Guru Nanak pictures a doctor taking the pulse of someone whose sickness is really the pain of separation from the Beloved, which no ordinary medicine can reach.
1102.tie_back: The Kural says ordinary illnesses have ordinary cures but love-sickness can be cured only by the beloved; Guru Nanak's foolish physician fails for the same reason, because the pain is love-longing.
1102.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1279, Raag Malar, Malar ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1102._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit: a sickness of the heart that medicine cannot touch; the Gurbani longing is the soul's spiritual separation from God, not romantic love.

1103.quote_or_event: “I do not seek power, and I do not seek liberation. My mind is in love with Your Lotus Feet.”
1103.explanation: In Raag Devgandhari, Guru Arjan says he wants neither kingship nor even mukti (liberation), only to stay in love with the Lord.
1103.tie_back: The Kural asks whether even the heaven of the Lotus-eyed god is sweeter than resting with one's beloved; Guru Arjan likewise puts loving closeness above every heavenly reward.
1103.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 534, Raag Devgandhari, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1103._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on preferring love to heaven or liberation; Guru Arjan's love is devotion to God, not human union, and Sikhism does not share the Kural's Vaishnava image of heaven.

1104.quote_or_event: “The month of Aasaarh seems burning hot, to those who are not close to their Husband Lord.”
1104.explanation: In his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Arjan says the scorching summer month burns those who are far from their Husband Lord, while those near Him find peace.
1104.tie_back: The Kural's fire burns when the lover moves away and cools when he comes near; Guru Arjan likewise says separation from the Beloved burns and nearness to Him cools.
1104.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 134, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1104._accuracy_note: Strong fit on separation as burning and nearness as relief; it is the bride-soul's spiritual longing for God, not romantic love.

1105.quote_or_event: “The Guru is the Sacred Shrine of Pilgrimage, the Guru is the Wish-fulfilling Elysian Tree.”
1105.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Arjan calls the Guru the parjat, the wish-granting tree of Indian legend, which gives whatever one desires.
1105.tie_back: The Kural says the beloved's embrace gives each desired joy exactly when it is wished for, an image the commentators link to the wish-granting tree; Guru Arjan uses that same tree for the Guru.
1105.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 52, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1105._accuracy_note: Partial match: the wish-granting tree image is shared, but it is applied to the Guru, not to a lover's embrace, and the Kural itself only implies the tree through its commentators.

1106.quote_or_event: “The dried branches are made green again in an instant.”
1106.explanation: In Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan describes the Guru's grace bringing spiritually withered people back to life at once, like dry wood putting out green shoots.
1106.tie_back: In the Kural each touch of the beloved makes the lover's wilting life sprout again; Guru Arjan uses the same picture of the withered made green.
1106.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 191, Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1106._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the shared image of withered life sprouting again; in Gurbani the reviving touch is the Guru's grace, not a lover's embrace.

1107.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has”
1107.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says the person who lives on honest earnings and shares part of them with others is the one who knows the true path (kirat karni and vand chhakna).
1107.tie_back: The Kural compares the beloved's embrace to eating one's own earned food in one's own home after sharing it; this is the Sikh ideal of honest work and sharing almost word for word.
1107.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1107._accuracy_note: Strong match for the Kural's simile of earning, sharing and then eating; the Kural uses it only as a comparison for love, whereas for Sikhs it is a core ethical teaching.

1108.quote_or_event: “They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies.”
1108.explanation: In Raag Suhi, Guru Amar Das says that true marriage is not just living side by side, but two people sharing one inner light.
1108.tie_back: The Kural praises an embrace so close that not even a breath of air can come between the two lovers; Guru Amar Das describes a union so close that two bodies share a single light.
1108.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Suhi, Suhi ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1108._accuracy_note: Strong fit on complete closeness between two people in love; Guru Amar Das stresses spiritual oneness in marriage rather than the physical embrace the Kural describes.

1109.quote_or_event: “O foolish and ignorant soul-bride, why are you so proud?”
1109.explanation: In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak gently scolds the bride-soul for her maan (sulky pride), which keeps her from her Husband Lord, and teaches that humility brings reunion.
1109.tie_back: The Kural names the lovers' quarrel, its making up and their coming together again as love's reward; Gurbani knows the same pattern of the bride's pride, reconciliation and reunion.
1109.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1109._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani treats the bride's pride as a fault to be given up, while the Kural enjoys the lovers' quarrel as a pleasure, and the Sikh love here is spiritual, not romantic.

1110.quote_or_event: “The more you say about them, the more there still remains to be said.”
1110.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says the greatness and virtues of God can never be fully described: every attempt only shows how much more there is.
1110.tie_back: The Kural says that, as with learning, every meeting with the beloved shows how much more there is to discover; Guru Nanak says the same about the endless Beloved, God.
1110.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 24), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1110._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on endlessness that is never used up; Japji speaks of describing God's infinite qualities, not of human love or learning.
